description: Time de Manaus no desafio Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. Vamos construir uma aplicação web que harmoniza os focos de calor dos sensores MODIS e VIIRS (dados do NASA FIRMS) num calendário de atividade de queimadas, pensada para alimentar alertas a comunidades e brigadas da Amazônia. Interesses: desenvolvimento web, análise e visualização de dados.
summary: We built a web app that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire hotspots into one consistent burning activity calendar for the Amazonas region. MODIS (2000–) and VIIRS (2018– on NOAA-20) see fire differently: VIIRS detects about 4× more hotspots, so stitching them creates a fake surge in fire. We measured the MODIS-to-VIIRS relationship for each month and for day and night passes in the years both sensors overlap, converted the MODIS archive to VIIRS-equivalent counts, and validated the conversion on a hidden year (2023: yearly error −0.2% vs −74% without harmonization). Anyone can pick an area (e.g., Autazes, Lábrea, Apuí) and see when fires usually happen, which years were worst, how a month compares with its historical median, and download the data as CSV. This historical context feeds our community alert assistant, Fogo Alerta, so warnings can reach riverside and rural communities before the fire season.
details: What it does. The app shows, for any area inside 10°S–2.5°N, 74°W–56°W (Amazonas state and surroundings): • a calendar (years × months, 2000–2025) of fire hotspots in one consistent unit (VIIRS-equivalent), with an accessible color ramp (inferno) and an anomaly view (purple–orange, colorblind-safe) comparing each month with its 2001–2025 median; • yearly totals for raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, the naive merge and the harmonized series, showing how harmonization removes the artificial jump when VIIRS begins; • the typical fire season (median and interquartile range) and any year compared with it; • key numbers: total hotspots, critical period of the year, most active year, last year vs. the median year; • a CSV download with the monthly series (raw sensor counts, harmonized counts, median and % difference); • an example of the alert text our Telegram assistant Fogo Alerta can send to community leaders and fire brigades using this context. How it works. (1) Data: NASA FIRMS country yearly summaries (standard processing) for Brazil — MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra and Aqua, 1 km, Nov 2000–Dec 2025) and VIIRS 375 m from NOAA-20 (2018–2025). We kept the region box and detections of type 0 (presumed vegetation fire), which removes static heat sources such as gas flares. (2) Aggregation: counts per 0.25° cell (~28 km), month, sensor and day/night pass (2,923,371 detections in total). (3) Harmonization: for each calendar month and pass, k = Σ VIIRS ÷ Σ MODIS over 2018–2025 (Terra-only factors for Nov 2000–Jun 2002, before Aqua). Before 2018, VIIRS-equivalent = k × MODIS (day and night separately); from 2018, observed VIIRS. Factors range from 2.3 to 9.4 (Terra+Aqua; Terra-only factors, used before Aqua started in July 2002, are higher); night factors are higher because VIIRS detects many weak night fires that MODIS misses. (4) Validation: we hid 2023, fitted the factors on the other overlap years, predicted 2023 from MODIS and compared with real VIIRS. We compared three variants (single ratio, monthly ratio with Terra+Aqua, monthly ratio with Aqua only) and kept the best. Results are shown in the app (chosen model: yearly error −0.2%, monthly error 3.1%, monthly correlation 0.999, cell-level yearly correlation 0.98; without harmonization the error is −74%. Refitting with 2018–2019 only, before MODIS orbit drift, changes pre-2018 totals by about −0.5%). We also report the VIIRS/MODIS ratio for each year to check the effect of MODIS orbit drift. Benefits. Fire managers, the Civil Defense, researchers and community brigades get a consistent 25-year view of when and where burning happens, can recognize unusual months quickly and can plan prevention before the critical period. VIIRS is the future of the record (MODIS is ending and Suomi NPP stopped delivering data in Nov 2026), so expressing the whole history in VIIRS units keeps the calendar valid going forward. Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy) for harmonization and validation; JavaScript (in-browser streaming loader for the FIRMS files); HTML/CSS/JavaScript with Leaflet and Chart.js for the static web app hosted on GitHub Pages. Limits and next steps. Hotspots are fire pixels, not fires or burned area; clouds and smoke hide fires; one regional factor per month and pass. Next: spatially varying factors (by vegetation or fire size, using FRP), NOAA-21, near-real-time updates for 2026, and connecting the calendar to Fogo Alerta's Telegram alerts. Demo: 7-slide PDF https://github.com/Samuelvf123/fogo-alerta-calendar/blob/main/demo/fogo-alerta-demo.pdf and 30-second video https://github.com/Samuelvf123/fogo-alerta-calendar/blob/main/demo/fogo-alerta-demo-30s.mp4 Code, data and validation report: https://github.com/Samuelvf123/fogo-alerta-calendar Use of AI: code and texts were written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant; the idea and approach came from the team, who reviewed the method and checked the results. This is stated in the app, the README and the code headers.
